title: Organizer deployment guide
html:
Goal: before the event, deploy one Launchpad environment with CloudFormation in every team's AWS account, check the models and the release policy, and hand each team its ConsoleUrl and the passwords of its five accounts; troubleshoot during the event; tear everything down cleanly afterwards. This page is for the organiser only; participants use nothing but a browser.

1. Delivery model

  • The default Region is us-east-1 (US East (N. Virginia)): every team's stack is deployed in us-east-1. The template maps CloudFront origin-facing prefix lists for us-east-1 and us-west-2 only, so it deploys in those two Regions only. This workshop's screenshots and the chapters' measured values come from a us-west-2 deployment; where a screenshot shows a Region (in ARNs, for example) it reads us-west-2, and a us-east-1 deployment shows us-east-1. The deployment duration was measured three times across the two Regions (section 3.1); with the current defaults (m9g.xlarge, the stack creates its own VPC) it took 13 min 44 s.
  • One AWS account per team, one stack per account. Several things the template creates have names that are unique per account + Region: the CloudWatch Logs resource policy AgentCoreLaunchpadTransactionSearch, the CDK stacks CDKToolkit and launchpad-base, the AgentCore gateways launchpad-gw / launchpad-kb-gw, the Memory launchpad_memory-* and the Registry launchpad-registry. A second stack in the same account and Region collides, and two teams would share one set of AgentCore resources.
  • Participants have no AWS access at all: no AWS console, no CloudShell, no access keys, no SSM. They only receive their team's ConsoleUrl (an HTTPS CloudFront address) and the passwords of the five console accounts. The only terminal step is the public API section of the Release chapter, which uses an API key issued by the console, not AWS credentials.
  • You (the organiser) deploy, check, hand out, troubleshoot and tear down in each team's account.

1.1 Architecture

In each team account, the template creates only the EC2 host and its network entry point. Everything else is created by the host's initialization script or by participants working in the console.

Component Purpose Created by (template / instance initialization / participant action)
CloudFormation stack agent-dlc-launchpad Entry stack the organizer deploys Organizer
Amazon CloudFront HTTPS address for the console (ConsoleUrl); adds the X-Launchpad-Origin-Key header on origin requests Template
VPC, public subnet, internet gateway, route Network for the host; you can pass a public subnet of an existing VPC instead (see 3.2) Template (skipped when you pass an existing VPC)
Security group Allows TCP 80 only from the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list Template
Amazon EC2 host nginx rejects requests without the origin key header (403); runs the Launchpad backend (FastAPI) and console frontend; SQLite ledger Template
IAM instance role AWS identity for the backend, cdk bootstrap, make bootstrap and everything participants do in the console Template (when ParticipantRoleArn is empty)
SQLite ledger data/launchpad.db All console data: registered accounts (passwords stored as salted PBKDF2-SHA256 hashes), permissions, agents, evaluations, release records, waivers, feedback and so on. It lives on the host's encrypted gp3 root volume and is deleted with the instance when the stack is deleted. The built-in admin is not in it; its password is in /etc/launchpad-auth.env Instance initialization (the backend creates it on first start; the init script writes the seeded accounts)
CDK stack CDKToolkit CDK assets bucket and ECR repository Instance initialization (cdk bootstrap)
CDK stack launchpad-base The S3, ECR, CodeBuild, Cognito and sample Lambda / API Gateway resources below, plus shared IAM roles Instance initialization (make bootstrap)
Amazon S3 launchpad-artifacts-* Agent packages, CodeBuild sources, knowledge base documents (kb/ prefix) Instance initialization (launchpad-base)
AWS CodeBuild launchpad-agent-builder Builds ARM64 images for the container path Instance initialization (launchpad-base)
Amazon ECR launchpad-agents Container images, scanned on push Instance initialization (launchpad-base); images are pushed when participants deploy
Amazon Cognito launchpad-users Gateway inbound auth (M2M client) Instance initialization (launchpad-base)
AWS Lambda / Amazon API Gateway Sample tools launchpad-hr-database and the office-facts REST API, used as gateway targets Instance initialization (launchpad-base)
AgentCore Registry launchpad-registry A2A registry records for agents Instance initialization (make bootstrap); records are created when participants deploy
AgentCore Memory launchpad_memory-* Agent memory Instance initialization (make bootstrap)
AgentCore Gateway launchpad-gw Exposes the sample tools as MCP tools Instance initialization (make bootstrap)
AgentCore Gateway launchpad-kb-gw Exposes knowledge base retrieval as MCP tools Participant action (first knowledge base attach)
AgentCore Identity Gateway outbound credential providers launchpad-office-facts-key, launchpad-gw-m2m, plus workload identities Instance initialization (make bootstrap)
AgentCore Runtime / Harness Lab agents: ZIP, container and BYOC deploys to Runtime; managed Harness Participant action
AgentCore Policy engine Cedar policies attached to launchpad-gw in the Release chapter (optional) Participant action
AgentCore Evaluations Evaluators and online evaluation Participant action
Amazon Bedrock models global.zai.glm-5.3 (lab agents) and global.openai.gpt-6-sol (judge), called through Converse Enabled in the account; instance initialization only probes them
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (managed) The lab knowledge base; ingests documents from S3 kb/ Participant action
CloudWatch Logs / X-Ray Transaction Search Runtime logs and the aws/spans span log group Template (Logs resource policy) + instance initialization (turns on Transaction Search)

2. Prerequisites

2.1 Accounts and permissions

Item Requirement
AWS accounts One per team, plus one for your own dry run (recommended). The account has never had this template in us-east-1 and has no CDK stack named launchpad-base
Identity that deploys the stack Can create a CloudFormation stack and its resources in each account: EC2 (VPC, subnet, route table, internet gateway, security group, instance; with an existing VPC only the security group and the instance, see section 3.2), a CloudFront distribution, an IAM role and instance profile (including iam:PassRole), a CloudWatch Logs resource policy (logs:PutResourcePolicy), and read the SSM public parameter /aws/service/canonical/ubuntu/... (to resolve the AMI). The simplest is a role with AdministratorAccess
Identity that troubleshoots and tears down The same role must also connect to the instance with Session Manager (ssm:StartSession), invoke Bedrock models (the check in section 5.3) and delete the stack
The instance's own permissions Nothing to prepare. With ParticipantRoleArn left empty, the stack creates the instance role itself, with the permissions of static/iam/participant-policy.json plus AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. The backend on the instance, cdk bootstrap, make bootstrap and everything participants do in the console reach AWS as this role

2.2 Bedrock models

In every team account, the following models should answer Bedrock Converse calls in us-east-1:

Model id Used by If it is missing
global.zai.glm-5.3 Every lab agent (lab-service-assistant, lab-policy-advisor, lab-canary-sandbox, option B's lab-legacy-agent); also the default model of a new agent The main line cannot run
global.openai.gpt-6-sol The judge model of the three custom evaluators (unicorn_fee_check, unicorn_privacy_guard, unicorn_no_overpromise); also the default Judge model of a new evaluator The Define chapter cannot create the evaluators, and every later step that uses them cannot score: the gate and judge calibration of the Evaluate chapter, the gate of the Release chapter, Score now and the scheduled regression of the Observe chapter, the regression run, online evaluation and gate of the Feedback chapter. Built-in evaluators (Builtin.*) are not affected
global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5 Platform features: the AI grouping of the Intent view (Observe chapter, section 6) and the try-chat suggested questions; and the optional option A container lab-legacy-container (Build chapter, section 3) The intent view falls back to mechanical grouping with the amber notice "The AI grouping was unavailable…"; suggested questions fall back to generic ones (no chapter uses them); option A deploys but cannot chat. The main line is not affected

The template also probes global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 as a fallback for the container path. The platform has a few more default models (simulated user global.openai.gpt-6-luna, architect global.openai.gpt-6-astra, global.openai.gpt-6-sol for the agents the architect assistant proposes, judge fallback global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5); no chapter uses those features.

  • Anthropic models require the account to have submitted its use-case details once: in the Bedrock console (us-east-1) → Model catalog, open the Claude model and submit the use-case details as prompted.
  • A third-party model may need an AWS Marketplace subscription on its first call. The instance role carries aws-marketplace:Subscribe, so its first call subscribes automatically; when you check with your own identity in section 5.3, that identity needs the permission too (AdministratorAccess includes it).

When these models are unavailable

Some accounts cannot invoke OpenAI or Anthropic models. Every model the platform itself calls is a setting you can switch to a model the account can invoke, without rebuilding the stack. Measured in us-east-1 on 2026-10-12: AgentCore Evaluations accepts global.zai.glm-5.3 as a judge model (global.moonshotai.kimi-k3 and DeepSeek R1 too), so an account without OpenAI can judge with GLM-5.3.

The template has already handled it once. When the setup script finds any of global.zai.glm-5.3, global.openai.gpt-6-sol, global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5 unavailable, it runs scripts/switch_models.py before the backend first starts: it picks the first working substitute for every model the platform calls, writes them to /etc/launchpad-models.env (the backend unit loads it through EnvironmentFile=-/etc/launchpad-models.env), and appends its output to /home/ubuntu/MODEL-ACCESS.txt after the probe results. A failure there never fails the stack; it leaves a WARNING: switch_models.py exited non-zero line in the log.

Option 1 (recommended): the Models page. Sign in to the team's console as admin (ConsoleUrl/v3) and click rail Modules → Configuration → Models. One row per setting shows the current model and its source (default, config, env = the file above, console).

  1. Pick a model in the row's select (the list is the text models this account offers in us-east-1).
  2. Click Test: one real, tiny call with that model. The two judge rows also have AgentCore Evaluations create a throwaway zz_probe_… evaluator and delete it, to confirm it accepts that judge; the simulated-user row checks forced tool choice.
  3. When the test passes, click Save: it applies at once, no restart. Reset undoes it; the row returns to the file or the default.

A choice saved on the console wins over /etc/launchpad-models.env.

Option 2: run the script on the instance (organizer). Open the SessionManagerUrl output and run in the instance shell:

bash
sudo -i
cd /home/ubuntu/agentcore_launchpad/backend
# probe and print what each setting would get; changes nothing
uv run --no-sync python ../scripts/switch_models.py --region us-east-1 --dry-run
# write /etc/launchpad-models.env and restart the backend
uv run --no-sync python ../scripts/switch_models.py --region us-east-1 --restart
  • --prefer global.zai.glm-5.3 makes every setting try GLM-5.3 right after its default.
  • Evaluators that already exist keep the judge they were created with. The script lists the ones whose judge no longer works; add --update-evaluators to move them to the chosen judge.
  • --restart restarts the backend and interrupts chats and evaluations in flight; do it between chapters.
  • Settings saved on the Models page are not affected by the file, and the script lists them; click Reset on the page for the file to apply.
  • Exit code 2 means some setting found no working model. The Claude-only features (the Claude Agent SDK of option A, Studio AI Fix) and the Skill Lab paths that run only on Claude or OpenAI are reported UNAVAILABLE in an account without those models and cannot switch to another model, but they do not count toward the exit code: on 2026-10-13 in us-west-2, simulating an account without OpenAI and Anthropic models, all five were UNAVAILABLE and the script exited 0. The chapters' main line does not depend on them.

A new judge model changes the scores. The measured results in the Evaluate and Release chapters come from a GLM-5.3 agent judged by GPT-6 Sol: with another judge, the scores, pass rates, confidence intervals and calibration κ of the judged criteria (C1, Q1, S1, S2 and so on) differ from the chapters' numbers, and so do the scores in the Observe and Feedback chapters. K1 (tokens per session) is a metric that no judge model decides, so the storyline of the release being held by K1 is unaffected. Without GLM-5.3, the default model of a new agent also becomes the substitute and the places where the chapters show global.zai.glm-5.3 show another model id; enable GLM-5.3 first if you can.

2.3 Service quotas

Quota This template's use (per account) Notes
EC2 Running On-Demand Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) instances (vCPU) 4 (one m9g.xlarge, 4 vCPU; the fallbacks m8g.xlarge, m7g.xlarge and m6g.xlarge are 4 vCPU too) A new account can have a low value; confirm ≥ 4 in the Service Quotas console before deploying
VPCs per Region 1 (0 when deploying into an existing VPC) Default 5; usually nothing to do
CloudFront distributions 1 Default 200
Bedrock tokens / requests per minute (global inference profiles of the three models) 4–5 people of one team chatting and running evaluations at once Evaluations replay the golden set concurrently
AgentCore Runtimes / Harnesses / Gateways About 5 agents and 3 gateways per team

3. Deploy one team's stack (CloudFormation console)

Do this once in every team's account. Do a complete dry run in your own account first, including the participants' Setup chapter.

  1. Download the template: launchpad-multiuser.yaml.

  2. Sign in to the team's account, switch the Region at the top right to US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1, and open CloudFormation → Create stack → With new resources (standard).

  3. Under Specify template choose Upload a template file, upload launchpad-multiuser.yaml, and click Next.

  4. Stack name agent-dlc-launchpad. Parameters:

    Parameter Value Notes
    ParticipantRoleArn Leave empty Empty means the stack creates the instance role. Only a Workshop Studio-provisioned account passes a participant role ARN; this workshop does not use that
    GitRepositoryUrl Keep the default https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-agentcore-launchpad.git The instance clones Launchpad from here
    GitBranch Keep the default console-v3 (the official repository's branch with the V3 console and Agent-DLC); for a scheduled event, a fixed tag Use the same branch or tag for every team so content and console match
    SelfRegistration Enabled (default) The Roles chapter demonstrates self-registration with admin approval; do not set Disabled
    InstanceType m9g.xlarge (default) Graviton (arm64), 4 vCPU / 16 GiB. The allowed values are, in order, m9g.xlarge, m8g.xlarge, m7g.xlarge, m6g.xlarge; pick a later one when the instance's Availability Zone does not offer the default. In us-east-1, us-east-1e and us-east-1f do not offer m9g.xlarge (measured with aws ec2 describe-instance-type-offerings; us-west-2 a–d all offer it). When the stack creates its own VPC, the subnet is in the Region's first Availability Zone (us-east-1a / us-west-2a), which is not affected
    RootVolumeSize 80 (default) GiB
    ExistingVpcId Leave empty (default) Empty means the stack creates its own VPC, public subnet, internet gateway and route table. With the id of an existing VPC (such as vpc-0123456789abcdef0), the stack creates none of these network resources and puts the security group in that VPC; requirements in section 3.2
    ExistingSubnetId Leave empty (default) Set together with ExistingVpcId, or leave both empty. The id of a public subnet in the ExistingVpcId VPC; the instance launches in this subnet. Requirements in section 3.2

  5. On Configure stack options, set Stack failure options to Preserve successfully provisioned resources. Then a failed setup does not roll the instance back, and you can still connect and read its log (section 8). Keep the rest at the defaults and click Next.

  6. At the bottom of the review page tick I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources. (the template creates the instance role and instance profile, which needs CAPABILITY_IAM), then click Submit.

Deploy with the AWS CLI (faster for many accounts)

Run in CloudShell (us-east-1) or in a local terminal with credentials for each account; set --profile to the team account's profile. file://launchpad-multiuser.yaml is a path relative to the current directory, so first change to the directory that holds the launchpad-multiuser.yaml downloaded in step 1; in CloudShell, upload the file to CloudShell first and run the command in the directory where it is:

bash
aws cloudformation create-stack \
  --region us-east-1 --profile team01 \
  --stack-name agent-dlc-launchpad \
  --template-body file://launchpad-multiuser.yaml \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM \
  --on-failure DO_NOTHING \
  --parameters ParameterKey=GitBranch,ParameterValue=console-v3

aws cloudformation wait stack-create-complete \
  --region us-east-1 --profile team01 --stack-name agent-dlc-launchpad

ParticipantRoleArn, GitRepositoryUrl, SelfRegistration, InstanceType, RootVolumeSize, ExistingVpcId and ExistingSubnetId take their defaults when not passed (without the two network parameters the stack creates its own VPC; for an existing VPC see section 3.2). --on-failure DO_NOTHING is the console's "Preserve successfully provisioned resources". The template is 45,211 bytes, under the 51,200-byte limit of --template-body.

3.1 What happens, and how long it takes

The stack starts in CREATE_IN_PROGRESS. WorkshopInstance waits until the instance has installed its dependencies, run cdk bootstrap and make bootstrap (the CDK stack launchpad-base plus the AgentCore Registry, Memory, Gateway and the rest), waited for Transaction Search to become ACTIVE, probed the four models, built the frontend, published the console, created the five accounts and set the release policy of workspace default to gated, and finally signalled success back to CloudFormation. The template allows 45 minutes for this (CreationPolicy PT45M); beyond that it fails. The CloudFront distribution ConsoleDistribution has no DependsOn in the template; it only uses the instance's public DNS as its origin through !GetAtt WorkshopInstance.PublicDnsName. The stack reaches CREATE_COMPLETE once both are done: WorkshopInstance has signalled success and ConsoleDistribution is deployed.

One measured run with the current template defaults (2026-10-13, us-west-2, InstanceType the default m9g.xlarge, the stack creates its own VPC, ParticipantRoleArn empty, submitted with the CLI command of section 3 with --region us-west-2):

Phase Time (UTC) Duration
Submit → VPC, subnet, security group, routes and instance role done 20:16:17 → 20:16:55 38 s
Instance profile ParticipantInstanceProfile 20:16:44 → 20:18:56 2 min 12 s
WorkshopInstance: launch → success signal (of which launchpad-base deploy 72 s) 20:18:57 → 20:26:53 7 min 56 s
CloudFront distribution ConsoleDistribution 20:26:54 → 20:30:00 3 min 6 s
Submit → CREATE_COMPLETE 20:16:17 → 20:30:01 13 min 44 s

In this run the instance was in us-west-2a and did not reboot during setup; launchpad-base was created in one go, with no Group not found. (section 8).

On the same day, a run in us-east-1 with the same default parameters, submitted with the section 3 CLI command as is (the stack created its own VPC; instance in us-east-1a, m9g.xlarge), took 13 min 41 s from submit to CREATE_COMPLETE: WorkshopInstance 7 min 56 s (launchpad-base deployed in 60 s) and the CloudFront distribution 3 min 4 s, essentially the same as the table above.

The two runs below are earlier measurements, with a different InstanceType or deployed into an existing VPC, for comparison.

One measured run (us-west-2, measured on an earlier build of console-v3, ParticipantRoleArn empty):

Phase Time (UTC) Duration
Submit → VPC, subnet, security group and instance role done 04:33:00 → 04:33:36 36 s
Instance profile ParticipantInstanceProfile 04:33:28 → 04:35:39 2 min 11 s
WorkshopInstance: launch → success signal (of which launchpad-base deploy 76 s) 04:35:40 → 04:44:36 8 min 56 s
CloudFront distribution ConsoleDistribution 04:44:38 → 04:54:18 9 min 40 s
Submit → CREATE_COMPLETE 04:33:00 → 04:54:19 21 min 19 s

A second measured run (2026-10-12, us-east-1, deployed into an existing VPC: the account's default VPC and its subnet in us-east-1a, submitted with the CLI command of section 3.2; measured on an earlier build of console-v3, ParticipantRoleArn empty; InstanceType m7g.xlarge, because this run was submitted before the default changed to m9g.xlarge):

Phase Time (UTC) Duration
Submit → security group, Logs resource policy and instance role done (no VPC or subnet items) 07:37:36 → 07:38:00 24 s
Instance profile ParticipantInstanceProfile 07:38:00 → 07:40:12 2 min 12 s
WorkshopInstance: launch → success signal (of which launchpad-base deploy 71 s) 07:40:12 → 07:48:28 8 min 16 s
CloudFront distribution ConsoleDistribution 07:48:30 → 07:52:35 4 min 5 s
Submit → CREATE_COMPLETE 07:37:36 → 07:52:36 15 min 0 s

The instance did not reboot during setup in this run (last -x reboot in the instance terminal shows a single system boot, the first one). Most of the difference between the three runs is the CloudFront distribution, which took from 3 min 6 s to 9 min 40 s; instance setup took between 7 min 56 s and 8 min 56 s.

3.2 Deploy into an existing VPC

When the stack should not create a VPC (the account's VPC quota is used up, or another team manages the network), deploy it into a public subnet of an existing VPC. The stack then creates only the security group and the instance (plus the CloudFront distribution, IAM role and Logs resource policy, which do not depend on the network), and no VPC, subnet, internet gateway or route table.

Requirements of the subnet and the VPC (all follow from how the template works):

Requirement Why Check (--region us-east-1, use your ids)
The VPC has both DNS hostnames and DNS resolution enabled The CloudFront origin is the instance's public DNS name (!GetAtt WorkshopInstance.PublicDnsName); in a VPC without DNS hostnames the instance gets no public DNS name aws ec2 describe-vpc-attribute --vpc-id vpc-… --attribute enableDnsHostnames and --attribute enableDnsSupport both return "Value": true
The subnet is public: its route table (the VPC's main route table when none is explicitly associated) has 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-… Instance setup needs the internet from its first command (apt, the AWS CLI installer, NodeSource, uv, npm, the GitHub clone, pip) and calls AWS APIs (the CloudFormation signal, Bedrock, AgentCore, CDK). CloudFront also reaches port 80 of the instance over the public internet aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-…; if that returns nothing, query the main route table with Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-… Name=association.main,Values=true; Routes must contain DestinationCidrBlock 0.0.0.0/0 with a GatewayId starting with igw-
The subnet belongs to the ExistingVpcId VPC The security group is created in ExistingVpcId, and the instance's network interface uses both that group and this subnet aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids subnet-… --query "Subnets[0].VpcId" equals ExistingVpcId
The subnet's Availability Zone offers InstanceType Otherwise EC2 refuses to launch the instance aws ec2 describe-instance-type-offerings --location-type availability-zone --filters Name=instance-type,Values=m9g.xlarge --query "InstanceTypeOfferings[].Location" lists the subnet's Availability Zone

The subnet's auto-assign public IPv4 address setting does not matter: the template sets AssociatePublicIpAddress: true on the instance's network interface, so the instance always gets a public IPv4 address. The security group's inbound rule is the same as with a new VPC: port 80 is open to the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list only.

CloudFormation cannot check at submit time that the subnet belongs to the VPC: the two parameters are of type String (the types AWS::EC2::VPC::Id / AWS::EC2::Subnet::Id do not accept an empty value, and empty means "create a VPC"), and that cross-parameter check needs those types. The template's Rules only check that the two are set together or left empty together. So check the third row of the table above before you submit.

Console: the parameter page of step 4 in section 3 shows the parameters in three groups; the last one is Network (optional), with two fields: Existing VPC id (leave empty to create a new VPC) (that is ExistingVpcId) and Existing public subnet id (required with an existing VPC) (that is ExistingSubnetId). Fill in both ids; the other steps stay the same.

CLI: add two entries after --parameters in the command of section 3. The command of the measured run (the account's default VPC and its subnet in us-east-1a; replace the two ids with your own):

bash
aws cloudformation create-stack \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --stack-name agent-dlc-launchpad \
  --template-body file://launchpad-multiuser.yaml \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM \
  --on-failure DO_NOTHING \
  --parameters ParameterKey=GitBranch,ParameterValue=console-v3 \
    ParameterKey=ExistingVpcId,ParameterValue=vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
    ParameterKey=ExistingSubnetId,ParameterValue=subnet-0123456789abcdef0

In this run both DNS attributes of the default VPC were true, the main route table had 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-…, and the subnet's zone us-east-1a offers both m7g.xlarge and m9g.xlarge. Measured result: the stack reached CREATE_COMPLETE in 15 min 0 s (phases in the second table of section 3.1) with only 7 stack resources (section 5.1 step 7); the instance got a public IPv4 address and the public DNS name ec2-…compute-1.amazonaws.com in the default VPC and its us-east-1a subnet; the checks of section 5 and section 1 of the Build chapter (developer deploys lab-service-assistant and gets an answer in Try it) all passed.

With only one of the two parameters set, the stack creates no resources and fails right away. Measured with only ExistingVpcId passed: stack status CREATE_FAILED, event reason Parameter validation failed: assertion error: Set ExistingVpcId and ExistingSubnetId together (deploy into an existing VPC), or leave both empty (the stack creates its own network).. Delete that stack and recreate it with both parameters.

Stacks for several teams can deploy at the same time without affecting each other (they are in different accounts).

4. Stack outputs

Open the stack's Outputs tab:

Output key Content Goes to
ConsoleUrl The console address https://dxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net The team
ConsoleUsername Always admin —
ConsolePassword admin's initial password (stops working once changed in the console, see section 6.6) The team
DeveloperPassword developer's password The team
BizOwnerPassword biz-owner's password The team
ReleaseOpsPassword release-ops's password The team
SmePassword sme's password The team
ConsoleAccounts One line naming the five accounts and their duties —
InstanceId, SessionManagerUrl, SessionManagerCommand, RepositoryPath, BootstrapLog Instance id, link / command for a shell on the instance, code location, command for the setup log Your own troubleshooting only

The passwords derive from the stack id, so every stack has its own. Fetch the values to hand out in one CLI call:

bash
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region us-east-1 --profile team01 \
  --stack-name agent-dlc-launchpad \
  --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='ConsoleUrl' || ends_with(OutputKey, 'Password')].[OutputKey,OutputValue]" \
  --output table

5. Check one team's environment

5.1 Stack and console

  1. The stack is CREATE_COMPLETE.

  2. Open ConsoleUrl/api/health in a browser. Expected result: {"status":"ok","version":"0.1.0","region":"us-east-1"} (version follows the Launchpad version).

  3. Open ConsoleUrl/v3 and sign in as admin with ConsolePassword. Expected result: V3's Command center, eyebrow COMMAND CENTER · DEFAULT · US-EAST-1 (指挥中心 · DEFAULT · US-EAST-1 in the Chinese UI; a us-west-2 deployment ends in US-WEST-2).

  4. Open ConsoleUrl/v3/workspaces. Expected result: the Default row with Region us-east-1, Tier DEV, Bootstrap status Ready.

  5. Open ConsoleUrl/v3/users. Expected result: besides admin, the four accounts developer, biz-owner, release-ops and sme, status Active, expiry Never expires.

  6. Open ConsoleUrl/v2?full=1 and scroll to the Service status card. Expected result: Gateway, Memory, Registry and Observability are Ready; Runtime reads "Lights up after the first deploy", Policy "Attach an engine in Governance", Evaluation "Lights up after the first evaluation".

  7. Only when deployed into an existing VPC (section 3.2): list the stack resources to confirm the stack created no network resources.

    bash
    aws cloudformation list-stack-resources --region us-east-1 \
  --stack-name agent-dlc-launchpad \
  --query "StackResourceSummaries[].[LogicalResourceId,ResourceType]" --output text

    Expected result (measured): 7 lines, ConsoleDistribution, NetworkReady (AWS::CloudFormation::WaitConditionHandle, a no-cost placeholder that makes the instance wait for the default route only when the stack builds its own VPC), ParticipantInstanceProfile, TransactionSearchLogsPolicy, WorkshopInstance, WorkshopInstanceRole, WorkshopSecurityGroup; no WorkshopVpc, PublicSubnet, InternetGateway, InternetGatewayAttachment, PublicRouteTable, DefaultRoute or PublicSubnetRouteTableAssociation. Those 7 network resources all carry the condition CreateVpc in the template and are created only when the stack builds its own VPC, which then gives 14 lines.

5.2 Release policy

In the browser where admin is signed in, open ConsoleUrl/api/release-policies/default. Expected result: policy is {"release_mode":"gated","calibration":{"period_days":30,"kappa_floor":0.6},"eval_cost_confirm_usd":5.0,"eval_cost_max_usd":20.0}. The setup log /var/log/workshop-bootstrap.log ends with four seeded … lines (the four member accounts), the line release policy: gated and the line member visibility: shared.

Then open ConsoleUrl/api/workspaces/default/settings/visibility. Expected result: {"resource_visibility":"shared"} (member visibility: shared). In the flywheel the agent developer builds is signed, labelled and released by biz-owner, release-ops and sme, so workspace default must stay shared: measured with isolated, all three accounts got 404 on developer's agent and its release record. Shared is the default anyway; the setup script still writes it explicitly and logs member visibility: shared.

5.3 Models

The setup script makes one real Converse call to each of the four models (maxTokens 16, retrying every 20 seconds up to 9 times on failure) and writes the result to /home/ubuntu/MODEL-ACCESS.txt on the instance, one line per model: available [bedrock] <model id> or unavailable [bedrock] <model id>. The stack fails outright only when none of the four answers; with only one missing it still succeeds and the log carries a WARNING: line. When one of the first three models is unavailable, the file also carries the output of scripts/switch_models.py: which model each setting got and which are reported UNAVAILABLE (see "When these models are unavailable" in section 2.2); the chosen models are in /etc/launchpad-models.env (read it with sudo cat).

To read the file, open the SessionManagerUrl output and run sudo cat /home/ubuntu/MODEL-ACCESS.txt in the instance shell.

You can also open CloudShell (us-east-1) in the team's account and call the models with your own identity:

bash
for MODEL in global.zai.glm-5.3 global.openai.gpt-6-sol global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5; do
  echo "== $MODEL"
  aws bedrock-runtime converse \
    --region us-east-1 \
    --model-id "$MODEL" \
    --messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"ping"}]}]' \
    --inference-config '{"maxTokens":512}' \
    --query '[stopReason, output.message.content[?text].text | [0]]' --output text
done

Expected result: under each == <model id> line, end_turn followed by the model's reply (a reply that contains line breaks spans several lines), with no AccessDeniedException / ValidationException. The wording changes from call to call. One measured output:

text
== global.zai.glm-5.3
end_turn	pong

I'm here and responsive. What can I help you with?
== global.openai.gpt-6-sol
end_turn	pong
== global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
end_turn	Hey! What's up? How can I help you today?

Give maxTokens 512: GLM-5.3 writes a reasoning block (reasoningContent) before its answer. With the setup script's 16, the measured call spent all 16 tokens on reasoning, ended with stopReason max_tokens, and the query printed None. The setup script only checks that the call succeeds, so it is not affected.

5.4 Walk the participant path in your dry-run account

In your dry-run account, complete Environment Setup and Console Tour and the first deploy and chat of Phase 2 · Build as a participant would, to confirm the models, the knowledge base and chat all work, before you send the access details to the teams.

6. Participant accounts

6.1 The five accounts the stack creates

Each stack creates five console accounts with fixed usernames; their passwords are in the stack outputs (section 4). The workshop plays out a team building a customer-service agent and taking it live, and the five accounts are the five kinds of people on that team. You don't need to have used the system: hand the accounts out by the "Give it to" column:

Account Give it to What they do in the workshop (plain terms)
admin The team lead or facilitator, ideally someone used to IT administration Runs the console itself: opens accounts for new members, grants permissions, resets forgotten passwords. Doesn't build the agent
developer Someone who codes or designs technical solutions Builds the agent: creates, deploys and chats with it; drafts the "acceptance criteria"; starts evaluations (the system scores the agent on a fixed set of test questions); asks to go live once it passes
biz-owner Someone who knows the business and makes decisions, such as a product manager or business lead Owns the bar: confirms and signs the acceptance criteria; maintains the set of test questions (called the "golden set" below); decides whether the AI judge that scores the agent can be trusted
release-ops Whoever is responsible for releases and stability, such as operations or a release manager Decides whether it goes live: signs the release after a passing evaluation, or blocks it; approves an "exception release" for a minor gap; rolls back to the previous version in one click if production goes wrong
sme A frontline expert in the details, such as a senior support agent or policy expert The "second grader": marks the same batch of answers right or wrong independently of biz-owner, and the system uses how well the two agree to check the AI judge

Why five accounts: the system checks "who may do what" per account. The person who builds the agent cannot sign its release, and the person who signs releases cannot change the acceptance criteria, just as development, business and operations check each other in a real team. So give each account to exactly one person and never share one.

biz-owner member criteria.sign (sign acceptance criteria), golden.admit (manage the golden set), judge.calibrate (decide AI-judge calibration)
release-ops operator —

The full description of roles and permissions is in Roles and Separation of Duties.

10. Tear down after the event

Follow this order, once per team account.

10.1 Participants clean up the console first

Ask every team to follow section 2 of Wrap-up and Cleanup: delete experiments and canaries, online evaluation, reviewer links, alerts, API keys, Cedar policies, every lab- agent, the knowledge base, registry records, custom evaluators and datasets in the console, and tell you when they finished.

10.2 Confirm the agents' AgentCore resources are gone

When an agent on live / candidate endpoints is deleted, the backend deletes the two named endpoints before the Runtime / Harness, retrying in the background every minute until AWS has let go. So let the backend on the instance finish:

  1. In the team's account open the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console (us-east-1) and look at the Runtime and Harness lists.
  2. Wait until every resource whose name starts with lab_ / lab- is gone (a managed Harness shows up in the Runtime list as harness_lab_…). In this run all four agents were gone within 4 minutes of the team confirming the deletions: a Runtime with live / candidate endpoints in under a minute, the Harness in about 2. For anything a team missed, delete its endpoints (live, candidate) in the console first, then the Runtime / Harness.
  3. On the knowledge bases page of the Amazon Bedrock console, check that lab-unicorn-policies is gone: a knowledge base deletes more slowly than an agent, about 10 minutes in this run.

Once a team has followed the Clean-up chapter and the background deletions on the AWS side are done, all that remains in AgentCore / Bedrock in us-east-1 in this run's account is the platform's shared resources (10.3 and 10.4 delete them):

Harness, online evaluation, custom evaluators, knowledge base None
Gateway launchpad-gw (targets office-facts, hr-database), launchpad-kb-gw (0 targets; the knowledge-base target went with the knowledge base), launchpad-exp-gw (0 targets)
Policy Policy engine launchpad_gw_policy (0 policies, launchpad-gw on LOG_ONLY)
Memory launchpad_memory-*
Credential providers launchpad-office-facts-key (API key), launchpad-gw-m2m (OAuth2)
Registry launchpad-registry (empty once the team has deleted its records)
Workload identities One each for the three gateways, the Skill Lab worker and the registry
IAM The per-agent launchpad-agent-lab-* roles went with the agents; what remains is the launchpad-base stack's roles, launchpad-skill-lab-worker and the instance role

10.3 Run the teardown script

The shared infrastructure make bootstrap created is not part of the CloudFormation stack, so deleting the stack does not delete it. The teardown script lives on the instance and runs with the instance role's permissions, so it must run before the stack is deleted (the instance role goes with the stack).

  1. Open the SessionManagerUrl output to get a shell on the instance.

  2. Switch to the ubuntu user and dry-run first:

    bash
    sudo -iu ubuntu
cd ~/agentcore_launchpad/backend
uv run python ../scripts/teardown.py --region us-east-1 --dry-run

    Expected result: within seconds, teardown targets (reverse creation order), listing in order: the gateway targets on launchpad-gw / launchpad-kb-gw ([gateway-target]), those two gateways ([gateway]), the credential providers launchpad-office-facts-key / launchpad-gw-m2m ([api-key-provider], [oauth2-provider]), the per-agent IAM roles starting with launchpad-agent- and tagged launchpad:agent-id (only if any are left), the AgentCore Memory launchpad_memory-* ([memory]), the AgentCore Registry ([registry], shown by id), the Skill Lab worker ([skill-lab-runtime], [skill-lab-role], only if used), and the CDK stack launchpad-base ([cdk-stack]). The last line is dry-run — nothing deleted (pass --yes to delete). After the team's clean-up this run listed 11 items: 2 targets, 2 gateways, 2 credential providers, the memory, the registry, the worker Runtime and role, and launchpad-base; no per-agent roles, because deleting the agents removed them.

    The per-agent IAM role entry lists every tagged agent role, including the roles of agents not deleted yet. If an [agent-role] line appears, an agent has not been deleted (or its deletion failed); go back to 10.1 first. IAM roles are not regional: if the same account also runs this stack in another Region, the roles of that Region's live agents are listed here too, and --yes deletes them, which breaks those agents. Have that Region's participants delete their agents as well before you run --yes.

  3. Once the list looks right, run it:

    bash
    uv run python ../scripts/teardown.py --region us-east-1 --yes 2>&1 | tee ~/teardown.log

    Expected result: one deleting [...] line per item, then CDK's event lines for deleting launchpad-base, ending with ✅ launchpad-base: destroyed and teardown complete (best-effort). In this run the whole --yes took 41 seconds, launchpad-base being the slowest (26 seconds): the S3 artifact bucket empties itself, the ECR repository launchpad-agents is force-deleted, and CodeBuild, the Cognito user pool and the shared execution role go with the stack. The line warning: `VIRTUAL_ENV=…` does not match the project environment path `.venv` in the output is a uv notice, not a failure; ignore it. An item that really fails prints warning: with the resource and the script carries on; run --dry-run and --yes again a few minutes later. A --dry-run straight after --yes may still list the Memory and the worker Runtime while they finish deleting in the background; run it again a little later and it prints nothing to tear down.

10.4 Delete what the teardown script leaves alone

Resource Where to delete it
The policy engine (attached to launchpad-gw in the Release chapter) The Policy page of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console
The shared experiment gateway launchpad-exp-gw (only after an A/B experiment) The Gateways page of the AgentCore console: delete its remaining targets (none once the team has cleaned up its experiments), then the gateway
Custom evaluators, online evaluation configurations (if a team missed them) The Evaluations page of the AgentCore console
Knowledge base lab-unicorn-policies (if a team missed it) The knowledge bases page of the Amazon Bedrock console

In this run the policy engine and launchpad-exp-gw were both gone within 40 seconds of deleting them.

10.5 Delete the stack

In CloudFormation (us-east-1) select agent-dlc-launchpad and click Delete.

The stack deletes: the EC2 instance and its encrypted EBS root volume, the CloudFront distribution, the VPC, subnet, route table and default route, internet gateway (with an existing VPC the stack did not create these four, and deleting the stack leaves the existing VPC, subnet, route table and internet gateway untouched), security group, the instance role the stack created (agent-dlc-launchpad-WorkshopInstanceRole-…) and the instance profile, and the CloudWatch Logs resource policy AgentCoreLaunchpadTransactionSearch. The CloudFront distribution has to be disabled before it can be deleted, which makes it the slowest item: in this run the whole stack deletion took 4 minutes (about 3 for CloudFront, 1 for everything else).

10.6 What stays in the account after the stack is gone

Resource Created by What to do
The CDK bootstrap stack CDKToolkit, with its asset bucket cdk-hnb659fds-assets-<ACCOUNT_ID>-us-east-1 and ECR repository cdk-hnb659fds-container-assets-<ACCOUNT_ID>-us-east-1 cdk bootstrap on the instance If the account runs no other CDK app, delete CDKToolkit in CloudFormation, then empty and delete the asset bucket (CDK keeps it by default) and the ECR repository by hand
CloudWatch Transaction Search (X-Ray trace segment destination set to CloudWatch Logs, and the CloudWatch Logs resource policy TransactionSearchXRayAccess placed when it is turned on) make bootstrap on the instance An account-wide setting that neither the teardown script nor the stack deletion touches (the stack only deletes its own resource policy AgentCoreLaunchpadTransactionSearch). Turn it off in the CloudWatch settings if nothing else in the account needs it
CloudWatch log groups: one per agent endpoint under /aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/ (including lab_legacy_container_* and the canary's stable* / treat*), one per online evaluation, experiment and canary evaluator under /aws/bedrock-agentcore/evaluations/results/, /aws/codebuild/launchpad-agent-builder, /aws/lambda/launchpad-hr-database, /aws/lambda/launchpad-base-CustomS3AutoDeleteObjects…, aws/spans, /aws/application-signals/data AgentCore, CodeBuild, Lambda and Transaction Search Delete them in CloudWatch Logs to clear them now; otherwise they expire with their retention (most have none set and stay)
IAM role launchpad-base-OfficeFactsApiCloudWatchRole…, with the API Gateway setting CloudWatch log role ARN pointing at it (the account has this setting separately in each Region) The sample REST API's default CloudWatch role in the launchpad-base stack (CDK creates it with a retain policy, so stack deletion skips it) One is left per deploy-and-teardown cycle. If no other API Gateway REST API in this Region needs execution or access logs, clear the log role in this Region's API Gateway settings, then delete the role it pointed at in IAM. Leave the role another Region's setting points at
Service-linked roles AWSServiceRoleForBedrockAgentCoreRuntimeIdentity, AWSServiceRoleForBedrockAgentCoreNetwork, AWSServiceRoleForAgentRegistry, AWSServiceRoleForCloudWatchApplicationSignals The first use of those services Usually kept; delete them in IAM once you are sure nothing else uses them
Bedrock model access and Marketplace subscriptions Section 2.2 Keep; they cost nothing

If the accounts were opened just for this event, the cleanest end is to close them once 10.3 is done.

11. Upgrade a deployed environment

An environment that is already deployed and in use does not need a new stack: upgrade it in place on the instance to the latest code of the official repository's console-v3. Accounts, agents, evaluation results and other data are kept (they live in the instance's SQLite ledger, and the backend upgrades its schema on start).

  1. In the CloudFormation console open Stacks → your stack → the Outputs tab and choose the SessionManagerUrl link: a Session Manager terminal opens in the browser. The prompt is $ (sh) and you are ssm-user; whoami confirms it.

    In the image: 1 the Outputs tab; 2 the SessionManagerUrl link, which opens the instance terminal. The five password outputs, the account ID, the CloudFront domain and the instance ID are masked.

    In the image: 1 the instance the terminal is connected to (the Instance ID matches the InstanceId output); 2 whoami returns ssm-user.

  2. Save the following as /tmp/lp-upgrade.sh: type cat > /tmp/lp-upgrade.sh, press Enter, paste, then press Ctrl+D on the new line:

    bash
    set -e
cd /home/ubuntu/agentcore_launchpad
cp data/launchpad.db data/launchpad.db.bak-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M)
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-agentcore-launchpad.git
git fetch --depth 1 origin console-v3
git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD
cd backend && uv sync
cd ../frontend && npm ci --no-audit --no-fund && npm run build

    In the image: 1 cat > /tmp/lp-upgrade.sh; 2 the pasted 8-line script; 3 after Ctrl+D the prompt $ returns and the file is written.

  3. Run it as the ubuntu user, then restart the services. The block below is one command joined with && \; paste it in one go and press Enter:

    bash
    sudo -u ubuntu -H bash -l /tmp/lp-upgrade.sh && \
{ grep -q launchpad-models.env /etc/systemd/system/launchpad-backend.service || \
  sudo sed -i '/^\[Service\]/a EnvironmentFile=-/etc/launchpad-models.env' /etc/systemd/system/launchpad-backend.service; } && \
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && \
sudo systemctl restart launchpad-backend && \
sudo systemctl reload nginx && \
curl -s --retry 10 --retry-connrefused --retry-delay 1 localhost:8000/api/health

    In the image: 1 the pasted command. The extra > characters between lines are the shell's continuation prompt interleaved with the pasted text; they don't affect the run. The script's output follows: git fetch gets console-v3, HEAD is now at …, uv sync.

Expected result: the frontend build prints ✓ built in … and the last line returns {"status":"ok","version":"0.1.0","region":"<your Region>"}, followed by the $ prompt. Two measured runs: us-east-1, upgrading from an earlier build, 30 seconds; us-west-2, from 5a79350 to 5a79350 (the instance was already on the latest console-v3 commit; backup, fetch, uv sync, npm ci, build and restart all ran as usual), 14.7 seconds from paste to the health check response.

In the image: 1 ✓ built in … (frontend build done) and the health check response {"status":"ok",…,"region":"us-west-2"}.

  • The ledger backup made by the step 2 script is data/launchpad.db.bak-<time>; if the upgrade goes wrong, stop the backend and copy it back.
  • The git remote set-url line points the code at the official repository; environments deployed earlier point at a repository that is no longer available, and git fetch fails without this line.
  • The EnvironmentFile line makes the backend read the configuration the model-switch script writes (section 2.2); environments deployed with the current template already have it, and the command skips it.
  • Everyone signs in again once after the upgrade.
  • Don't split step 3 into separate lines pasted together: sudo on the instance has use_pty enabled, so while the first sudo runs it swallows the lines pasted after it; they are echoed but never run (measured: the script finished, but the backend was not restarted and no health check was printed). The single command joined with && \ above is read in full by the shell before it runs.
  • Don't run multi-line commands as sudo -iu ubuntu bash -lc '…': over SSM the multi-line quoting is split and the command fails. Write them to a script file first, as above.
